title: Scaling Federated Learning Across Docker, Kubernetes, and Slurm with NVIDIA FLARE | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA FLARE 2.8/2.9 splits federated learning into persistent federation services plus ephemeral job workers launched through Docker, Kubernetes, or Slurm, so no participating institution has to standardize on a common platform. The strategic point is that NVIDIA is inserting itself as the coordination layer for cross-organization AI training on regulated data (hospitals, universities) without owning the data or the schedulers.

insights.claim: NVIDIA FLARE splits a federated-learning deployment into long-running server/client parent processes that coordinate the federation and transient job workers that actually execute training, so coordination processes never sit on idle GPUs.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: GPU utilization is the binding cost in federated deployments; architectures that keep control planes off accelerators raise effective GPU ROI and reduce the number of GPUs a hospital or university must dedicate to participate.
insights.quote: The parent processes can remain available without occupying the GPUs required for training.
insights.locator: Separating federation coordination from job execution

insights.claim: FLARE job workers are created on demand and exit when their work completes, converting federated-learning compute from a standing reservation into a burst allocation governed by the local scheduler.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: Lower standing-capacity requirements widen the addressable base of institutions that can join federations, expanding NVIDIA's footprint into sites that could not justify dedicated clusters.
insights.quote: The worker receives the job, uses the requested resources, returns its results, and exits when its work is complete.
insights.locator: Separating federation coordination from job execution

insights.claim: Separating the FLARE parent container image from the job container image lets infrastructure owners freeze the platform runtime while researchers independently update training frameworks and model code, decoupling platform upgrade cycles from research velocity.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: Reduced upgrade coupling is the classic adoption unlock for enterprise IT; it lowers the institutional veto that usually kills multi-party ML projects.
insights.locator: Docker for containerized execution on one host

themes.theme: Heterogeneity as design premise, not obstacle

insights.claim: Requiring every participant in a federated-learning collaboration to adopt the same infrastructure makes platform standardization a prerequisite for collaboration, which is the practical reason multi-institution AI projects stall.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: Whoever removes the standardization prerequisite captures the coordination layer for regulated-data AI; watch for the same pattern in healthcare, finance, and government consortia.
insights.quote: Requiring every participant to adopt the same infrastructure can turn platform standardization into a prerequisite for collaboration.
insights.locator: That operational complexity grows when organizations

insights.claim: A single FLARE federation can run Docker at one site, a Kubernetes cluster at another, and Slurm at a research center simultaneously, with each site remaining the resource authority over its own compute.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: This is explicitly a bet that on-prem HPC (Slurm) and cloud-native (Kubernetes) estates will stay fragmented rather than converge, which favors orchestration-agnostic tooling over any single scheduler vendor.
insights.locator: Deploy job workers with Docker, Kubernetes, and Slurm

insights.claim: In FLARE's Slurm integration the cluster scheduler retains full authority over accounts, partitions, QoS rules, cgroups, filesystem permissions, and device controls, so federated jobs are governed by exactly the same policy machinery as non-federated HPC workloads.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: Preserving the incumbent operational model removes the administrator objection that normally blocks new frameworks on shared academic GPU clusters — the main install base for medical AI research.
insights.quote: This preserves the operational model that cluster administrators already use for non-federated workloads.
insights.locator: Slurm for scheduled GPU and multi-node allocations

themes.theme: Studies as multi-tenancy and data governance boundary

insights.claim: FLARE 'studies' create a logical multi-tenant boundary inside one deployment, scoping job visibility, client status, submission targets, and deployment maps to whichever study an admin session is opened against.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: Multi-tenancy is the gating feature that lets one institutional deployment amortize across many research projects, improving the unit economics of federated infrastructure.

insights.claim: Jobs submitted into a FLARE study cannot choose arbitrary local dataset paths or supply secret values; a site-owned local/study_runtime.yaml maps the study to approved dataset mounts, images, and secret references while the server verifies study membership before the job reaches a site.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: This is the compliance primitive that makes hospital data custodians signable; it converts federated learning from a research demo into something a legal team can approve.
insights.quote: The jobs do not choose arbitrary local dataset paths or supply secret values.
insights.locator: A data scientist selects the study

insights.claim: In the Kubernetes launcher, secret_env entries become Kubernetes secretKeyRef references so credential values never leave the site's own secret store while still reaching the study worker's environment.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: Credential-by-reference is what allows a third-party framework to touch regulated infrastructure without becoming a data-handling party itself — a liability-shaping design choice.
insights.quote: The configuration contains references to Secrets, not their values.

insights.claim: NVIDIA explicitly limits studies to organizations sharing one FLARE server and PKI, and tells anyone needing a separate PKI, separate infrastructure administrator, or independent failure blast radius to run entirely separate deployments.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: A vendor naming the limits of its own isolation model signals that the highest-trust cross-competitor use cases still require duplicated infrastructure — a cost line buyers should model rather than assume away.
insights.quote: Organizations that require a separate PKI, infrastructure administrator, or failure blast radius should use separate FLARE deployments.

themes.theme: Portable resource abstraction and release cadence

insights.claim: FLARE 2.9 introduced a portable resource_spec in a job's meta.json using only three keys — num_of_gpus, num_of_cpus, and memory — which each site's launcher translates into Docker nano_cpus and mem_limit, Kubernetes requests and limits, or Slurm --cpus-per-task, --mem, and --gres flags.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: A minimal portable resource vocabulary is how a framework becomes the lowest common denominator across schedulers; it is the same wedge Kubernetes used against bespoke orchestrators.

insights.claim: FLARE's resource spec supports an @default profile inherited by every targeted site with per-site overrides, so in NVIDIA's own example two hospitals inherit one GPU, four CPU units, and 64 GiB while a university overrides to eight GPUs and the server to zero GPUs.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: The example reveals the expected asymmetry of real federations — academic centers contribute 8x the GPU of clinical sites — which is where the compute demand actually lands.
insights.locator: The @default entry applies one resource profile

insights.claim: Deployment-runtime support shipped incrementally rather than all at once: Docker and Kubernetes support arrived in NVIDIA FLARE 2.8 and Slurm support only in FLARE 2.9.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: HPC/Slurm support landing last indicates the academic and national-lab channel is only now being opened, so adoption metrics from that segment are early-stage and forward-looking.
insights.quote: Docker and Kubernetes deployment support is available in NVIDIA FLARE 2.8. FLARE 2.9 adds Slurm support.

insights.claim: NVIDIA draws an explicit security division of labor in which FLARE supplies participant authentication, secure communication, and authorization, while each site's own execution platform enforces workload isolation, approved images, secrets, and access controls.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: Vendors that push isolation validation onto the customer keep liability low but raise buyer integration cost; assess whether target institutions actually have the ops maturity to hold up their side.
insights.quote: Site operators configure host and cluster security, approved images, secrets, and access controls, and validate workload isolation for their chosen runtime.

insights.claim: A pathology study spanning two hospitals and a university can run GPU workers while a parallel outcomes study restricted to only the hospitals runs CPU workers on structured clinical data, both sharing the same persistent federation services.
insights.speaker: Peter Cnudde
insights.so_what: Not every federated study pulls GPU demand — structured-data studies stay on CPU — so federated-learning adoption converts into accelerator demand unevenly by modality.
